newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge ties Ruiz Massieu fortune to drug money.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge ties Ruiz Massieu fortune to drug money.

text.p: A U.S. federal judge on Thursday said more than $9 million deposited in the Texas bank account of former Mexican Deputy Attorney General Mario Ruiz Massieu most likely came from bribes paid by drug traffickers.

The ruling followed testimony of a government informant who described placing two suitcases full of drug money in the trunk of Ruiz Massieu's car during a 1994 rendezvous outside the Mexican Attorney General's headquarters in downtown Mexico City.
"Mr. Massieu was aware that the money was being placed in his car and was aware of the source of the money," U.S. District Judge Nancy Atlas said.

Attempts by Ruiz Massieu to transfer the money in the Texas account to a Swiss bank after he fled Mexico in the face of narcotics-related charges in March 1995 also indicated "that the money was not legally derived," Atlas said.

The ruling capped the first half of a two-part civil forfeiture proceeding in which U.S. prosecutors are trying to seize the $9 million Texas Commerce Bank account opened by Ruiz Massieu in December 1993.

In the balance of the civil case, Ruiz Massieu is expected to present witnesses who will testify that the money was legally obtained and should be returned to him. In court filings, Ruiz Massieu has said the money consisted of government bonuses and part of a family fortune placed in the United States for safekeeping in the event of political or economic turmoil in Mexico.

Between late 1993 and early 1995, Jorge Stergios, an aide to Ruiz Massieu, made 25 deposits to the Texas account consisting of hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash -- most of that in $20 bills wrapped in rubber bands and cellophane.
"The predominant denominations were $20s, street money if you will," Robert Whelan, a U.S. Internal Revenue Service drug task force investigator said on Thursday.

In earlier testimony, Raul Macias, a former bodyguard for a Mexican police commander, said he placed two suitcases filled with cash in the trunk of a blue Ford Grand Marquis and recognised Ruiz Massieu as a passenger in the car.

The money consisted of proceeds from more than 10 tons of Colombian cocaine seized by Mexican police from a large plane at a remote airstrip in Sombrerete, Zacatecas in northern Mexico. The drugs, which were being transported by convicted drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego, were then sold back to drug traffickers, Macias said.
A U.S. Customs agent also testified that informants said the former Mexican deputy attorney general had taken bribes from powerful drug lords, including Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
Witnesses in the civil trial in Houston have described widespread corruption that included bribes paid by drug traffickers "all the way to the top in Mexico City."
